Transcription resistive is stamped by H3K36me with almost undetectable transcription activity but open-chromatin state, and occupies most documented plant essential genes. Mutating SDG8, previously known as the major H3K36 methyltransferase in Arabidopsis, surprisingly elevates 78.7% of H3K36me3-marked resistive loci, which accounts for 39.4% of the coding genome. Genetically, SDG8 prevents H3K36me activity of SDG4 at short and intronless genes to secure plant fertility, while it collaborates with other H3K36me methyltransferases The transcription states in eukaryotic genomes mainly include activation and repression, which involves numerous regulation machineries. Transcription repression, also termed transcription silencing, is often associated with the heterochromatin domain in the genomes1. The heterochromatin state can be achieved through DNA methylation and repressive histone modifications, and displays a highly compacted chromatin state, finally leading to inaccessibility to RNA polymerases. The constitutive heterochromatin is mainly found in the non-coding genome and consists of repetitive sequences, transposable elements and ribosomal DNA, with the presence of highly methylated DNA and histone H3 lysine 9 (H3K9me2/3) as well as lysine 27 (H3K27me1)2,3. The facultative heterochromatin, which is usually located in the coding genome, is marked by trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 27 (H3K27me3), is principally catalysed by polycomb repressive complexes 2 (PRC2), is interspersed in the eukaryotic genome and is related to developmental genes4,5.

SDG8, also known as EFS (EARLY FLOWERING IN SHORT DAYS), is reported as the main H3K36me3 methyltransferase in Arabidopsis, and its functional mutations have been shown to cause a global decrease in H3K36me3 levels15–17, resulting in numerous developmental defects17–21. However, the dynamics and regulation of different H3K36 methylation forms are still a mystery in plants. In this study, we started with the genome-wide characterization of H3K36me3 and surprisingly observed that mutation of SDG8 can lead to substantially elevated levels of H3K36me3 in the coding genome of Arabidopsis. Furthermore, we unexpectedly found that a large proportion of the coding genome exists as a chromatin state that is open chromatin, marked by H3K36me3, occupied by RNA polymerase II, and looked similar to the ready-for-transcription state but with little to no transcription activity (similar to the level of silencing), even with heat stimulation. We termed this chromatin state ‘transcriptional resistive’, which is distinctive from traditional transcription activation and transcription silencing. Our data reveal a previously undiscovered function of H3K36me3 and transcription regulation.

text: To dissect the functions of the H3K36 methyltransferases in Arabidopsis on catalysing different forms of H3K36 methylation (Fig. 1a), we started with the analysis of H3K36me3 chromatin immunoprecipitation and sequencing (ChIP-seq) using Arabidopsis seedlings and profiled the enrichment signal on protein-coding genes (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1a). Relative to the wild type (WT), the mutants sdg4, sdg25, sdg26 and atxr2 (see materials for more details) showed decreased levels of H3K36me3 around the transcription start site (TSS); however, the sdg8 (efs-3)19 mutant displayed increased levels of H3K36me3 from the TSS to the gene bodies (Fig. 1b). We identified a series of protein-coding genes with differential H3K36me3 modification [DMGs, log2(fold-change (FC)) > 1.4 or <−1.4, FDR (false discovery rate) < 0.05] in these five mutants, and found that only the sdg8 mutant showed a larger portion of increased DMGs than decreased DMGs (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1b). These results were further validated by ChIP–qPCR (Extended Data Fig. 1d). Furthermore, we checked and compared the numbers of DMGs among mutants of other HMTs that are responsible for H3K4me3, H3K9me2, H3K27me1 and H3K27me3 in Arabidopsis. No other mutants of HMTs could lead to numerous upregulated DMGs as the sdg8 mutant does (Fig. 1c). Therefore, the observation that highly elevated H3K36me3 levels exist in the sdg8 mutant encouraged us to explore the extended functions of SDG8.

text: Furthermore, we found that SDG8 is highly expressed during germination and in pollens (Extended Data Fig. 2a), and this was validated by quantitative PCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR) with different tissues (Extended Data Fig. 2b). In addition, we performed the H3K36me3 ChIP-seq using germinating seeds (48hS + 24hL, 48-h stratification and 24-h growth under normal condition), cauline leaves and pollen of wild-type Col-0 and checked the H3K36me3 levels in comparison to that in seedlings (lowly expressed SDG8) (Extended Data Fig. 2c). Lower abundance of H3K36me3 was observed in the germinating seeds and pollens, the developmental stages with highly expressed SDG8 compared with the other two tissues (Extended Data Fig. 2c–f), indicating the role of SDG8 in inhibiting H3K36me3 deposition. To further determine the regulatory role of SDG8 in H3K36me3, we carried out in-depth analysis and clustered all the protein-coding genes on the basis of the H3K36me3 enrichment in the sdg8 mutant compared with wild-type Col-0 (Fig. 1d and Methods). The genes in Cluster 1 showed a total absence of H3K36me3 modifications (C1, totally SDG8 dependent, n = 1,670), and Cluster 2 genes displayed decreased H3K36me3 levels in the sdg8 mutant (C2, partially SDG8 dependent, n = 1,236). However, the genes in Cluster 3 (C3, SDG8 restraining, n = 10,710) exhibited the accumulated H3K36me3 levels around the TSS in the absence of SDG8 (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 1d). More than half of protein-coding genes in the Arabidopsis genome were marked by H3K36me3 modifications, and 78.7% of these belong to Cluster 3 (Fig. 1e), indicating a potential role of SDG8 in inhibiting the excessive deposition of H3K36me3 in genes. To confirm this observation, we purchased another two H3K36me3 antibodies from Active Motif (AM_61902 and AM_61022 in Supplementary Fig. 1) and performed the ChIP-seq and data analysis. The data using these two H3K36me3 antibodies could still generate clustered genes similar to those in Fig. 1d (Supplementary Fig. 1), further confirming our findings that H3K36me3 levels were increased in C3 genes of the sdg8 mutant. In addition, we generated CRISPR/Cas9-based knockout plant materials with the SET domain of the SDG8 abolished (sdg8-SET-KO in Extended Data Fig. 3) and conducted H3K36me3 ChIP-seq assay. The sdg8-SET-KO mutant contains a 554-bp deletion in the genomic DNA within the SET domain (Extended Data Fig. 3a) but does not alter the reading frame in the other region of SDG8 mRNA (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c), which creates a truncated SET domain based on the Sanger sequencing of the products of PCR with reverse transcription (RT–PCR) (amino acids truncation from I976 to E1089 on SDG8 protein, Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). Four clustered genes were generated using H3K36me3 ChIP-seq data of the sdg8-SET-KO mutant with our standard of classification, and the C3_sdg8-SET-KO genes also showed elevated H3K36me3 levels (Extended Data Fig. 3e,g). In addition, 95.7% (6,898/7,210) of C3_sdg8-SET-KO genes overlapped with the C3 genes in Fig. 1d (Extended Data Fig. 3f), suggesting that abolishing only the SET domain in SDG8 could also lead to elevated H3K36me3 on C3 genes.

text: We also reanalysed the published H3K36me3 ChIP-seq data of Col-0 and another allelic mutant of SDG8, sdg8-5 (ref. 17) and plotted H3K36me3 levels on the C1–C4 genes. The results also showed that the H3K36me3 levels of C3 genes are elevated in sdg8-5 (Extended Data Fig. 1e). Combining with the SDG8-HA ChIP-seq data17, we found that higher relative abundance of SDG8 binding was observed in the C1 and C2 genes (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1f). Interestingly, although SDG8 binding in the C3 genes is highly enriched compared with random genes, the binding affinity is comparable to that of C1 and C2 genes (Fig. 1f). Together, these results support the idea that H3K36me3 modification on C1–C3 genes is directly modulated by SDG8.

text: To dissect the functions of SDG8 in modifying different methylation states of H3K36, we performed H3K36me1 and H3K36me2 ChIP-seq in Col-0 and sdg8 mutant, and plotted these three states of H3K36me in C1–C4 genes (Fig. 1g and Extended Data Fig. 4a). The results showed that H3K36me1 are less abundant than H3K36me2 and H3K36me3 in Col-0, and SDG8 is mainly responsible for the deposition of diand trimethylation on H3K36 in C1 and C2 genes, preferring to catalyse H3K36me2 on the 3’-terminal region and H3K36me3 on the 5’-terminal region of these genes, respectively (Fig. 1g and Extended Data Fig. 4b,e). Interestingly, the level of H3K36me2 is elevated preferably in 5’-terminal regions of C3 genes in the sdg8 mutant, which is similar to the pattern of H3K36me3 in sdg8 compared to Col-0, and H3K36me1 levels are also slightly elevated in C3 genes of sdg8 (Fig. 1g and Extended Data Fig. 4b), suggesting a non-methyltransferase function of SDG8 in suppressing methylation on H3K36 in Arabidopsis. text: Next, we performed association analysis of clustered genes with various chromatin, and the results showed that the C1–C3 genes are highly co-localized with active transcription markers (Fig. 1h), leading us to further investigate the transcription state of these clustered genes. Consistent with the known function of H3K36me3 that is associated with active transcription, RNA-seq analysis revealed that a larger portion of genes in SDG8-dependent C1 and C2 was downregulated in the sdg8 mutant (Fig. 2a). However, the C3 genes showed no discernible preference in the mRNA levels between the wild-type Col-0 and sdg8 mutant (Fig. 2a), even though there are increased levels of H3K36me3 on C3 genes of sdg8 compared with wild type, suggesting that H3K36me3 abundance on C3 genes are not correlated with promoting gene expression. Since C3 genes comprise the majority of H3K36me3 (78.7% of total H3K36me3-marked genes, Fig. 1e), we were curious about their transcription state. First, we evaluated the open-chromatin states via the assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with high-throughput sequencing (ATAC-seq), and found that comparable levels were displayed in the wild type and sdg8 mutant (Fig. 2b). To precisely determine the transcription state of C3 genes, we performed native elongating transcripts sequencing (NET-seq) that can capture the nascent transcripts by RNA polymerase on chromatin22. The NET-seq results uncovered that there was a decreased activity of transcriptional elongated Pol II (Ser2P Pol II) at C1 and C2 genes in sdg8 compared with wild type (Fig. 2c), in line with their decrease in H3K36me3 (Fig. 1d), indicating that the C1 and C2 genes are marked by the transcription-coupled H3K36me3. Unexpectedly, almost no activity of Ser2P Pol II was observed on C3 genes in both wild-type Col-0 and sdg8 mutant (Fig. 2c), which is inconsistent with the well-known functions of H3K36me3 in enhancing transcription elongation7,8. To unveil whether the defects in transcription elongation on the C3 gene were derived from the transcription initiation stage, we used anti-Ser5P Pol II antibodies for NET-seq to detect the nascent RNAs in transcription initiation.

Together, the results above revealed that, even though C3 genes in sdg8 displayed many active transcription features, including an open-chromatin state (Fig. 2b), active histone modification markers (Fig. 1h) and high RNA abundance (Extended Data Fig. 5a), the transcription activity on these genes was highly inhibited, indicating that the accumulated H3K36me3 in sdg8 marked 39.4% of total coding genes that exhibit the ability for transcription but with no reaction to transcribe. We termed this state ‘transcription resistive’, as the open-chromatin states seem to resist the transcription machinery; furthermore, ‘resistive’ shares the same suffix, ‘-tive’, as Active, Facultative and Constitutive (see below Fig. 3c). To exclude the possibility that facultative heterochromatin silencing, similar to H3K27me3 modification, could mark the transcription-resistive genes and is involved in transcription inhibition, we conducted H3K27me3 ChIP-seq assay in Col-0 and sdg8 mutant. The data showed no clear difference in H3K27me3 enrichment on the protein-coding genes (Supplementary Fig. 2a,b), indicating that SDG8 does not affect H3K27me3. Notably, there was little to no H3K27me3 enrichment on the C3 genes in Col-0, and the level was not altered in sdg8 (Supplementary Fig. 2a), suggesting that the transcription-resistive state is not caused by H3K27me3 deposition and that the low to no transcription at resistive loci is completely different from PRC2-mediated gene silencing.

text: To understand why there are high levels of mRNA abundance but little to no RNA polymerase activities on C3 genes (Fig. 2c,d), we analysed the RNA degradome23 and mRNA half-life data24 on the clustered genes. The profiling of 5’ monophosphate ends (5’ P ends) of RNA degradation intermediates, a method to detect the target of 5’ to 3’ RNA decay pathway, showed results wherein the RNAs from C3 genes tended to be much less degraded compared with RNAs from C1 and C2 genes (Fig. 2e). In addition, the average mRNA half-life of C3 genes was significantly higher than those of the other clustered genes (Fig. 2f,g), although the portions of m6A-modification in C1–C3 mRNA are comparable (Extended Data Fig. 5b). text: Given that a large portion of C3 genes display the transcription-resistive state (Fig. 2b,c), we moved to investigate the transcription-resistive genes in the wild-type Col-0 genome. The protein-coding genes with Pol II binding (Pol II ChIP-seq) or open-chromatin state (ATAC-seq) but ultra-low Ser2P signal (NET-seq with anti-Pol II Ser2P antibody), and without H3K27me3 markers (facultative genes) were defined as transcription-resistive genes (see details in Supplementary Fig. 3). In a parallel manner, the protein-coding genes with Pol II binding or open-chromatin state (ATAC-seq) and high Ser2P signal were defined as transcription-activation genes (see details in Supplementary Fig. 3 legends). H3K27me3-marked facultative genes were used as a control. Overall, we identified 4,375 TA genes and 12,911 TR genes in the genome (Supplementary Fig. 3). Permutation test showed that the TR and TA genes are both negatively associated with repressive chromatin markers but highly positively associated with transcriptionally active chromatin markers (Fig. 3a). Notably, the TR genes show much more correlation of methylation of H3K36 modifications than TA genes, especially the H3K36me3 modification (Fig. 3a), suggesting that the methylation on H3K36 could mark a large number of protein-coding genes with the newly defined chromatin state, transcription resistive.

text: To test the possibility that the transcription rate of TR genes is too rapid to be effectively captured by NET-seq, we conducted flavopiridol (FLA, 10 μM) treatment (1 h) to slow down the Pol II elongation rate28,29 and then performed NET-seq using anti-Pol II Ser2P antibody. Results showed that the Ser2P signals on the majority of TA genes were indeed reduced upon FLA treatment (Extended Data Fig. 7), suggesting that FLA treatment can slow down the transcription rate of the transcription-active genes. However, there is no obvious difference in Ser2P NET-seq signals on the majority of TR genes between the control and FLA (Extended Data Fig. 7), indicating that the Ser2P signal on TR genes cannot be captured even when transcription elongation is inhibited, excluding the possibility that the transcription rate of TR genes is too rapid to be effectively captured by NET-seq. In detail, we defined a group of protein-coding genes as transcription resistive, accounting for 47.5% of total protein-coding genes in the Arabidopsis genome, and showing active chromatin states similar to transcription-activation genes (n = 4,375, accounting for 16.1% of protein-coding genes) (Fig. 3b,c) but with little to no transcription activities similar to heterochromatin, including the H3K9me2-marked constitutive heterochromatin genes (n = 259, accounting for 1% of protein-coding genes) and H3K27me3-marked facultative heterochromatin genes (n = 6,280, accounting for 23.1% of protein-coding genes) (Fig. 3b,c). Moreover, using similar parameters, we identified 7,198 TR genes in the mouse (Mus musculus) genome (Supplementary Fig. 4a), although they are not tightly associated with H3K36me modifications (Supplementary Fig. 4b,c, see details in the Discussion).

text: To provide notable insights into the biological functional relevance of the TR genes, we performed integrated analysis of H3K36me3 ChIP-seq, Pol II ChIP and RNA stability on TA and TR genes. The coding genes are categorized into 4 quartiles (q1 to q4 genes) on the basis of the mRNA half-lives data (Extended Data Fig. 8a). We then plotted the H3K36me3 ChIP-seq signals on q1–q4 genes, which are accompanied by increased mRNA stabilization, and observed that H3K36me3 correlates with increased transcript half-life (Extended Data Fig. 8b). Moreover, the TR genes, which accumulated more H3K36me3 than TA genes (Fig. 3a), were also associated with increased transcript half-life (Extended Data Fig. 8c). Together, these results indicate that H3K36me3 could serve as a chromatin signal to stabilize TR transcripts. Within the analysis combining Pol II ChIP-seq (including Pol II, Pol II Ser2P and Pol II Ser5P) (data from GSE181489) with TA/TR genes, the TA genes displayed a higher enrichment of all types of Pol II signal, which is consistent with the feature of active transcription in TA genes (Extended Data Fig. 8d). In addition, the TR genes showed a relatively high enrichment of Pol II Ser2P signals (Extended Data Fig. 8d), suggesting a potential stalling during the transcription elongation phase and finally resulting in very low transcription activities in TR genes.

Results revealed that genes regulated by SDG25 had H3K36me3 levels that were substantially lower in sdg8 sdg26, while genes regulated by SDG26 were enriched in the region in sdg8 sdg25 with lower H3K36me3 (Extended Data Fig. 10g, top). Collectively, the results showed that, although SDG25 and SDG26 have highly overlapping regulatory sites for H3K36me3 modification, their functions are not consistent, possibly due to preference or tightness of binding to one or two enzymes (see model in Extended Data Fig. 4f). In addition, we checked the transcription activities of sdg8 sdg25 sdg26 compared to sdg8 via NET-seq. Results showed that the transcription activities over C3 genes with decreased H3K36me3 in sdg8 sdg25 sdg26 compared with sdg8 sdg25 (Extended Data Fig. 10h, top) or sdg8 sdg26 (Extended Data Fig. 10h, bottom) remained subtle in sdg8 sdg25 sdg26 compared with sdg8 (Extended Data Fig. 10h), suggesting that the resistive state of these genes was not disturbed in seedling stages. text: Since the sdg8 sdg4 double mutant exhibited dramatically decreased H3K36me3 levels compared with sdg8 on C3 genes (Fig. 4a–c), we then focused on the effect of SDG4 on ‘transcription resistive’. We performed NET-seq using sdg4 and sdg4 sdg8 mutants and found that the transcription activities are elevated on C3 genes in the sdg4 sdg8 compared with sdg8 as well as sdg4 single mutants, although the levels are still low (Fig. 4e, see also Figs. 2c and 3b). In addition, these increased Pol II activities in the sdg4 sdg8 are mostly performed on the short and intronless genes, Groups 1 and 2 genes (Fig. 4d), whose H3K36me3 deposition is largely dependent on SDG4 activity in the absence of SDG8 (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 9d,e,g,h), suggesting that the H3K36me3 dynamics mediated by SDG4 and SDG8 could modulate the transcription, leading to a transcription-resistive state. In the absence of both SDG4 and SDG8, the decreased H3K36me3 promotes the activity of transcription on C3 genes (Fig. 4b,e and Extended Data Fig. 9b,e), further suggesting that H3K36me3 could function as the transcription suppressor. A previous study showed that both SDG8 and SDG4 are highly expressed in the sperm nuclei of the pollen31. To confirm the relationship between SDG8 and SDG4, we decided to test whether altering the abundance of one protein will affect the enrichment state of the other. Therefore, we performed immunofluorescence assays to detect the enrichment of SDG8 and SDG4 in the sperm nuclei of pollens. Results showed that both SDG8 and SDG4 proteins are enriched in the sperm nuclei of Col-0 pollens (Extended Data Fig. 9f), while the SDG4 is more accumulated in the sperm nuclei of the sdg8 pollens (Extended Data Fig. 9f, left). Consistently, SDG8 is also more stimulated in the sperm nuclei of sdg4 pollen compared with Col-0 pollen (Extended Data Fig. 9f, right), suggesting a competitive relationship between these two methyltransferases.

Moreover, we also checked the upregulated mRNA in sdg8 sdg4 compared with sdg8, and overlapped them with the upregulated nascent RNAs in sdg8 sdg4 compared with sdg8. Finally, a total of 1,350 genes were identified to be upregulated in transcription activities and RNA abundance (Fig. 4f), and these genes, whose resistive state was disturbed in the sdg8 sdg4, are associated with the reproduction process of plants (Fig. 4g). Consistently, sdg8 sdg4 showed obvious developmental defects during reproductive growth, even though these double mutants did not show visible abnormal phenotypes in seedling stages (Fig. 4h). We observed that the floral organ in sdg8 sdg4 exhibited more defects than in the sdg8 single mutant; the stamen and pistil in sdg8 sdg4 were both shorter than those in the wild type or single mutant, finally resulting in inadequate development of siliques (Fig. 4h).

text: The precise regulation of transcription is essential for faithful development among species. Active transcription often features open chromatin, Pol II enrichment and active histone modifications, while transcription silencing is tightly associated with compacted chromatin states and repressive histone modifications, such as H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 (Fig. 3c). In this study, we identified a novel transcription state, termed ‘transcription resistive’, which shares active histone markers with transcriptionally active genes but displays the undetectable transcription activities of silencing genes (marked by H3K27me3 and H3K9me2). Importantly, the majority of resistive genes are essential for plant development (Fig. 2h) and disruption of the transcription-resistive state on these genes could cause severe plant phenotypes (Fig. 4h). Moreover, this transcription-resistive state seems to be conserved among species (Extended Data Fig. 6 and Supplementary Fig. 4). It is well documented that H3K36me3 is associated with transcription-active genes and functions as a transcription elongation-coupled epigenetic marker7,8. However, in our case, H3K36me3 has an additional role with respect to transcription-resistive genes (Fig. 3), which is not coupled with active transcription. Even in the sdg8 mutant, the much more stimulated H3K36me3 did not trigger 816 transcription (Fig. 1d); however, the loss of H3K36me3 modifications on some short genes in the sdg4 sdg8 double mutant stimulated transcriptional activities (Fig. 4b–e), unveiling an astonishing role of H3K36me3 in transcription inhibition.

text: This finding is different from observations in mammals where the gene body H3K36me3 could recruit DNA methyltransferase Dnmt3b for the establishment of gene body DNA methylation to prevent cryptic transcription initiation32, as the transcription resistive in our case is not correlated with DNA methylation (Fig. 3a). In Neurospora crassa, ASH1, one of the H3K36 methyltransferases, mediated H3K36me2-marked genes, which are poorly transcribed, as these genes are co-marked by facultative heterochromatin markers H3K27me2/3 (ref. 33). In addition, the loss of SDG26, a homologue of SDG8 in Arabidopsis, was reported to promote H3K36me3 levels and transcription levels on FLC gene independently of its histone methyltransferase activity, although accompanied by reduced H3K27me3 modifications34,35. However, the resistive genes that we found are not associated with H3K27me3 modification (Fig. 3a), and the H3K27me3 modification was not altered in the sdg8 mutant (Supplementary Fig. 2).
section: Discussion
title: H3K36 methylation stamps transcription resistive to preserve development in plants

text: In mammals, a single methyltransferase, SETD2, is responsible for dito trimethylation of H3K36 (ref. 6). In plants, there are multiple methyltransferases for implementing H3K36 methylation (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 6a), and a single methyltransferase could catalyse multivalent H3K36 methylation (this study and refs. 11,12,14,16), indicating more complicated crosstalk among H3K36 methyltransferases in plants, which may explain why the transcriptional-resistive state in mammals is not tightly correlated with H3K36 methylation (Supplementary Fig. 4). SDG8, the major H3K36 methyltransferase in Arabidopsis, is associated with multiple transcription activators, such as H3K4me1/2 (ref. 36), H3K27me3 demethylase ELF6 (ref. 37) and active forms of RNAPII, but it also interacts with inactive forms of RNAPII38, suggesting that H3K36 methylation, mainly regulated by SDG8 in Arabidopsis, could be involved in an unusual establishment of the chromatin environment or transcription state. In addition, it is worth mentioning that no H3K36me demethylases have been identified in plants until now. Therefore, the crosstalk or competitive cooperation among multiple methyltransferases may trigger a special monitoring system to keep proper H3K36me levels throughout the plant genome, which does not necessarily require any H3K36me demethylases. We propose that the complicated crosstalk among multiple H3K36 methyltransferases could regulate the low-to-zerolevel transcription of ‘transcription resistive’ in plants. Future work is needed to reveal more conserved factors participating in ‘transcription resistive’ among species.

text: ChIP for histone modifications was carried out on the basis of published protocols40. In brief, 2 g of 14-day-old seedlings were cross-linked with 1% formaldehyde. The cross-linking was stopped by adding 0.125 M glycine and the sample was rinsed 5 times with double-distilled H2O. Then the plants were frozen with liquid nitrogen, ground into fine powder and lysed with Honda buffer (containing 0.44 M sucrose, 12.5% Ficoll, 2.5% dextran T40, 20 mM HEPES KOH pH 7.4, 10 mM MgCl2, 0.5% Triton X-100, 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride, 1% plant protease inhibitor cocktail, 5 mM dithiothreitol). The homogenate was filtered through Miracloth (Millipore, 475855-1R) and then spun at 2,000 g for 15 min. The nuclear pellet was washed twice with the same buffer mentioned above and resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 10 mM EDTA, 1% SDS, 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride and 1× protease inhibitor) and sonicated using a Bioruptor Pico with the following settings: 30 s on/ off intervals, 4 times for 10 min each. The sample was spun at maximum speed for 10 min. The supernatant was collected and diluted 10-fold with ChIP dilution buffer (1.1% Triton X-100, 1.2 mM EDTA, 16.7 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 167 mM NaCl). The diluted chromatin solution was incubated with 5 µg of anti-H3K36me1 (Abcam, ab9048), anti-H3K36me2 (Abcam, ab9049), anti-H3K36me3 (Abcam, ab9050) or anti-H3K27me3 (Millipore, 07-449) at 4 °C overnight. Then, 25 μl Dynabeads Protein G magnetic beads (Invitrogen, 10004D) were added to each sample and the sample incubated for 3 h to perform immunoprecipitation. The beads were washed with 1 ml of low-salt wash buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.8, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 0.1% SDS, 1% Triton X-100) once, with 1 ml of high-salt wash buffer (wash buffer with 500 mM NaCl) twice, with 1 ml of LiCl buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.8, 1 mM EDTA, 0.25 M LiCl, 1% sodium deoxycholate) once and with 1 ml of TE buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 1 mM EDTA) once. Chelex resin (100 μl, 10%; BioRad, 1422842) was added to the immune complexes and the complexes incubated at 95 °C for 10 min at 1,300 r.p.m. to elute them. The sample was brought to room temperature and incubated with 1 μl proteinase K (20 mg ml−1, Thermo Fisher) at 45 °C for 1 h. The sample was then boiled at 95 °C for 10 min and spun at 1,300 r.p.m. The eluted DNA was purified with phenol-chloroform before DNA library construction. DNA acquired from ChIP were sonicated to 250-bp fragments using focused ultrasonicator (Covaris, M220). The Accel-NGS 1S Plus DNA Library kit (Swift Biosciences) was used to construct ChIP-seq libraries from the sonicated DNA, following manufacturer instructions. The libraries were verified on an Agilent BioAnalyzer and then sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 system.

The nuclear pellet was resuspended once with HBB buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.6, 0.44 M sucrose, 10 mM MgCl2, 817 0.10% Triton X-100 and 10 mM β-mercaptoethanol) and once with HBC buffer (4/5 vol. HBB + 1/5 vol. glycerol), and then resuspended in MNase buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 5 mM NaCl and 2.5 mM CaCl2), with 20 U of micrococcal nuclease (Takara, 2910A) added. The reaction mixture was incubated at 37 °C for 8 min, and 19 mM EDTA was added to stop the reaction. Sonication was performed with 1 s on/off for 10 cycles after MNase digestion, and the supernatant was collected by spinning at maximum speed. The supernatant was incubated with beads coated with 10 μg antibody (anti-Pol II Ser5p, Abcam, ab5131; anti-Pol II Ser2p, Abcam, ab5095) for 2 h at 4 °C, and the complexes were washed 8 times with chilled NET-2 buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl and 0.05% NP-40). Finally, the beads were resuspended in T4 polynucleotide kinase (T4 PNK) reaction mixture with 97.5 μl of T4 PNK buffer, 1 μl of T4 PNK enzymes (NEB, M0236) and 1.5 μl of 100 mM ATP, and then incubated at 37 °C for 10 min at 1,400 r.p.m. Then, the supernatant was discarded and beads were washed with NET-2 buffer. The beads were resuspended again in 500 μl of TRIzol and incubated for 10 min at room temperature. After chloroform extraction, RNA was precipitated with 1/10 volume of NH4OAc, 3 volumes of ethanol and 1 μl of GlycoBlue (Invitrogen). The NEXTflex small RNA-Seq Kit V3 was used to construct the libraries from the precipitated RNA.

text: The ATAC-seq method was modified from previous publications42,43. Briefly, 0.25 g of 14-day-old seedlings were freshly collected and ground with a homogenizer in ice-cold nuclei purification buffer (20 mM Mops pH 7.0, 40 mM NaCl, 90 mM KCl, 2 mM EDTA, 0.5 mM EGTA, 0.5 mM spermidine, 0.2 mM spermine and 1× protease inhibitor cocktail). The homogenate was filtered with a 40-μm nylon mesh and then centrifuged to discard the supernatant. The nuclear pellet was sequentially purified with NEB2 buffer (0.25 M sucrose, 10 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 10 mM MgCl2, 1% Triton X-100 and 1× protease inhibitor cocktail), NEB3 (1.7 M sucrose, 10 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 2 mM MgCl2, 0.15% Triton X-100 and 1× protease inhibitor cocktail) and nuclei purification buffer. The nuclear pellet was resuspended in DEPC-treated H2O and then immediately subjected to transposition reaction. Chromatin was fragmented in the reaction system containing 5 μl TTE Mix V5, 10 μl of 2× DMF buffer (66 mM Tris-acetate pH 7.8, 132 mM K-acetate, 20 mM Mg-acetate and 32% DMF) at 37 °C for 30 min. Fragmented DNA was purified with the ChIP DNA Clean & Concentrator kit (Zymo, D5205). The purified DNA was used for library construction.
